segments.text: AI makes mistakes, and when it does, it uses the exact same confident voice it uses when
the facts are perfectly accurate.
But even an answer with no factual errors can still fall short.
It might generate a joke that isn't funny, an explanation that leaves you confused, or
a business plan that simply won't work in the real world.
To filter out those bad results, you need to ask two core questions of every single
response.
Is it right, and is it good enough for what I need?
You can't just ignore AI.
The technology is too powerful to leave on the shelf.
To be smarter than the tool, you have to develop the systematic evaluation skills required
to grade its homework.
This is the quick pass.
It is the mandatory first step for every single AI response before you put it to work.
It starts with reading.
If you pass AI-generated information along, you are responsible for what it says.
You also can't judge an answer you don't understand.
If a section is confusing, ask the AI to explain that specific paragraph in simpler terms until
you grasp it completely.
Next, you validate.
Compare the answer against what you already know, and check it against your original prompt.
You are looking to see if anything is factually wrong, if crucial context is missing, or if
the format just isn't useful for your task.
The absolute bare minimum action required before using any AI output is right here.
Read, understand, and validate.
Once you complete the quick pass, you move to this phase, deciding if the answer requires
a deeper investigation.
Start by asking if you can actually judge the output.
Compare the answer with your existing knowledge.
If you lack the foundational expertise to verify it yourself, commit to checking it further.
Next, look at the kind of task.
A factual summary requires precise accuracy, an email needs clear writing, a plan needs
viability, evaluate based on what matters most for the job.
Finally, assess the real-world stakes.
A movie recommendation has low risk, medical advice carries high stakes.
What happens if this answer is wrong?
Your scrutiny must proportionally match the task's risk.
Give the answer the attention it deserves.
When an answer does require a closer look, you enter the dig phase.
This is a specific toolkit of checks you can apply.
First, ask the AI for its sources and actually open them to verify their reliability.
Second, challenge the AI directly.
Ask, what's the strongest argument against this, to expose hidden weaknesses?
You can also search for omitted context.
Ask the AI, what important information did you leave out?
Doing this uncovers details that might entirely alter your perspective.
If the tool has browsing capabilities, ask it to search the live web for current information,
and verify the links match the claims.
Sometimes you must step outside the system entirely.
Recalculate numbers by hand, test code, or consult a human expert.
Use AI to help check, but you are the final arbiter of reality.
After your evaluation is complete, you reach the final phase, making an actionable decision
based on your results.
If the answer is proven accurate and fully meets the requirements of your task,
you choose the first option.
Use it. Put it to work.
If it's close, fix it.
Instruct the AI on what needs to change or edit the text yourself,
and check the revision before applying it.
Finally, if the AI is proving unhelpful, you choose to walk away.
Abandon the tool and seek alternative methods or human expertise.
The tool answers, but you evaluate.
The human user retains all authority and responsibility for the final product.
Let's apply this to a high-stakes scenario.
Imagine an AI claims a scholarship deadline is March 1st.
You check the sources.
The official webpage and the school calendar both clearly state the deadline is February 15th.
Because the actual evidence contradicts the AI's claim, you choose to fix it,
operating entirely on the February 15th deadline.
The answer generated by an AI is not the evidence.
It is merely a claim that requires proof.
As a final reminder, the tool answers you evaluate.
Read, understand, validate.
